records.title: Eryndor — Planetary Fundamentals
records.summary: A five-continent, magically alive world, approximately 50,000 km in diameter.
records.body:
Eryndor is approximately 50,000 km in diameter and 157,080 km around. Its surface is 60% water and 40% land. A 24-hour day, 360-day year, and four roughly 90-day seasons govern the working calendar.

The older 13,400-km diameter, 42,000-km circumference and 71%-water model are superseded.

Everyday gravity, hydrology, weather, agriculture and biology behave as on Earth, by explicit creator decision. The world is magical; no further physical justification for familiar gravity is required unless the creator later requests one.

records.title: The Five Continents
records.summary: Avarra, Tharvorn, Sahrad, Orundel, Vaelora.
records.body:
Avarra contains Karak-Varn and the established Hammerfeld characters; a new campaign starting location has not yet been selected. Tharvorn is northern, Sahrad southern, Orundel eastern and Vaelora western. Every continent contains multiple peoples, states and traditions.

Twin Titans dry-land shares: Avarra 32%, Orundel 28%, Tharvorn 12%, Sahrad 12%, Vaelora 11%, islands and separate archipelagos 5%. No island territory should be counted twice. Coastlines, countries, mapping scales and precise intercontinental routes await further survey.

records.title: World Tone and Creative Rules
records.summary: Dark and gritty yet hopeful; no species is uniformly good or evil.
records.body:
Eryndor contains exploitation, conquest, famine, prejudice and catastrophic loss, alongside friendship, celebration, scholarship, rescue and reform. Consequences matter. Fantasy-scale cities and heroes are allowed without requiring Earth-historical ceilings.

Long-lived peoples can have large families; birth rates are not silently adjusted. A person may devote a century to a craft or choose domestic life; cultures have distinct expectations. No single trait determines everyone in a people. The creator can revise accepted canon with explicit supersession and a retained change log.

records.title: Ages Versus Eras
records.summary: Worldwide Ages are not the same as continent-specific historical eras.
records.body:
Five worldwide Ages are recognized; the current one is the Fifth Age. Each civilization may name and subdivide historical time differently. The Second Age's Awakening, Wonder and Fire divisions are Avarran conventions, not mandatory world calendars.

The Era of Crowns in the Fifth Age has a documented year-numbering convention; the former campaign date (Autumn Day 22, Year 3847) is retired and is not the new campaign start date. Era of Crowns years must not automatically be counted from the global beginning of the Fifth Age.

records.title: Current World Population
records.summary: 2.0628 billion modeled residents across 28 numerical categories.
records.body:
The current sixfold planning census contains 2,062,800,000 modeled residents: Avarra 1,019,760,000; Tharvorn 171,000,000; Sahrad 282,222,000; Orundel 393,600,000; Vaelora 196,218,000. This replaces a 343.8-million draft.

Global Khazari 144 million, Eldar 108 million, Urakai 186 million, humans 960 million. The Seven Khazari Throne domains total 132 million and are INCLUDED within worldwide Khazari; Karak-Varn's 22.8 million are included within the Thrones. Drakari, Aelwyn and Living Mountains are not precisely enumerated.

This is a worldbuilding resimulation, not sudden births or a confirmed omniscient census. Metro-versus-domain boundaries need reconciliation.

CANON — AVARRAN SECOND-AGE BIRTH BOOM (2026-11-22): Across Avarra's peoples, the birth rate was at least 2× each people's ordinary baseline during the Era of Awakening (Second Age Years 1–321) and Era of Wonder (Years 322–1321), falling to approximately 1.5× baseline during the Era of Fire (Years 1322–1437). These are BIRTH-RATE multipliers, NOT multipliers of population totals; the population may keep rising after the birth rate falls. Khazari remained asleep for all of Awakening and awakened gradually during Years 322–488; they participate only from awakening onward, not during Years 1–321. This event is specific to Avarra and is not automatically imposed on the other continents. Ordinary baseline birth rates, previously established long lifespans, existing present-day population totals, and populations of other continents are NOT changed by this historical note. Population-size consequences, migration, mortality, disasters and subsequent-age demographics require a separate continuity audit.

CANON KHAZARI GEOGRAPHIC DISTRIBUTION (2026-11-22): The overwhelming majority of Khazari live in Avarra's Ironspine mountain system, the core homeland of the Seven Thrones. Only a few scattered pockets exist outside Avarra, primarily in some of the larger mountain ranges on other continents. Smaller Khazari settlements elsewhere within Avarra may exist, but no extensive overseas Khazari realm is implied. Exact percentages, population totals, and overseas settlement histories remain undecided pending demographic revision. The older 132-million Seven Thrones figure counts domain residents and must not automatically be equated to 132 million ethnic Khazari.

CANON KHAZARI DISTRIBUTION PERCENTAGES (2026-11-22): Of the WORLDWIDE Khazari population, 83% live in Avarra, including 74% living directly within the Ironspine mountain system and 9% elsewhere in surrounding Avarran regions; the remaining 17% live across other continents, principally in mountain ranges. These are percentages of the global Khazari population, NOT percentages of Avarra's population or of the 83% subgroup. Total worldwide Khazari headcount remains provisional pending demographic recalculation. Continuity review needed: the earlier description 'only a few scattered pockets outside Avarra' must be interpreted as geographically concentrated overseas settlements or revised, because 17% of the species is a significant minority. Do not invent overseas kingdoms or settlements without creator approval.

records.title: First Age
records.summary: Its length is unknown and no authentic contemporary records survive.
records.body:
Its length is unknown and no authentic contemporary records survive. Old stories describe extraordinary prosperity, but their historical accuracy is unverified. It ended when the First Great Cataclysm destroyed or shattered moons. Lost moon-specific magics did not return.

Creator clarification (2026-11-21): Multiple moons collided, initiating the Great Cataclysm at the end of this Age; the collision trigger is established canon, not speculation.

records.title: First Great Cataclysm
records.summary: Multiple moons collided, triggering the Great Cataclysm and ending the First Age.
records.body:
Multiple moons collided, initiating the Great Cataclysm that ended the First Age and overturned the world's civilizations and lunar magical order. Destroyed source-moons permanently ended their associated magical disciplines; fragments of some shattered bodies became new moons and sources of new magic. The initiating multiple-moon collisions are established canon. Exact participating moon count, collision sequence, wider cascade and subsequent astronomical details remain open.

CREATOR REOPENED FOR EDITING (2026-11-21): All aspects of the Great Cataclysm, including the multiple-moon collision trigger, sequence, extent, lunar magic consequences and dating, may be reconsidered. The above describes the previous established version, preserved for comparison; do not treat the collision mechanism as newly immutable canon while revisions are underway.

CREATOR'S NEW HISTORICAL DIRECTION (2026-11-21; under development): The First Throne was a vast subterranean Khazari empire centered in the Ironspine Mountains. The inland sea enclosed by the mountain ring is linked to a mysterious magical harness or power system that the First Throne learned to use. Its exploitation precipitated the Great Cataclysm and the empire's fall. The catastrophe, the Silence Below and the eastern mine are to have connected histories; precise mechanisms, sequence, dates, and nature of the mine connection are deliberately undecided. The previously established multiple-moon collision scenario is under revision: do not assert whether collisions caused the catastrophe or were caused by the harness until decided. This is a working historical direction, not license to invent missing details.

CREATOR CONFIRMATION (2026-11-21): The First Throne discovered an extraordinary naturally occurring magical power beneath the Ironspine Mountains, then engineered and constructed a vast artificial harness to exploit it. The inland sea is connected to this system, but its precise role (source, regulator, consequence, or other) remains undecided. Exploitation of the system ultimately triggered the Great Cataclysm and contributed to the empire's fall. The failure mechanism, lunar collision relationship, and eastern mine/Silence Below connection remain open; do not invent these details.

CREATOR CONFIRMATION (2026-11-21): The inland sea BOTH contains and naturally regulates the extraordinary magical power. Without any artificial harness it can accomplish wondrous things but remains unpredictable. The First Throne's Khazari sought to control and exploit that power; dwarven greed for mastery and power is a thematic cause of their overreach. The artificial harness's interference with natural regulation precipitated the Great Cataclysm and the empire's fall. Greed is an imperial motivation, not a universal moral property of all Khazari. Exact engineering, failure mechanism, moon collisions and mine/Silence Below linkage remain open.

CREATOR HISTORICAL DIRECTION (2026-11-21): The eastern mine's ancient deeper workings are components of the First Throne's immense magical harness connected to the inland sea; this is why their unusual engineering attracts investigation. An immensely powerful Balrog-like (analogy only, not a Tolkien Balrog) being was SENT into the depths to stop the machine and is now locked/sealed there. The being's sender, origin, nature, alignment, actions, exact sealing agent, and whether the harness was fully stopped remain undecided. Preserve the difference between being sent to stop the machine and being responsible for causing the Cataclysm. Present-day investigation does not revive erased Gloin gameplay.

CREATOR REFINEMENT (2026-11-21): The powerful sealed being was sent not merely to stop the First Throne's harness, but to STOP AND PUNISH the dwarven empire itself for its greed and overreach in trying to control the inland sea's power. This is a punitive intervention against the First Throne's actions, with an atmosphere reminiscent of Tolkien's Balrog but an original Eryndor being, not literally a Balrog. The sender, mandate's exact scope, creature's identity, when it arrived, deeds, and sealing remain open. Do not reduce its mission to a technical machine shutdown or assume all Khazari were guilty.

CREATOR CANON CLARIFICATION (2026-11-21): The First Throne is ALREADY FORGOTTEN by the Second Age for magical reasons tied to the Great Cataclysm. Second Age Khazari do not consciously know of the First Throne or found the Seven Thrones as deliberate successors to it. Shared ancestral heritage, surviving structures, traditions and machinery may persist without remembered provenance. The exact memory-erasure mechanism, geographic scope, exceptions, persistence, and whether anyone retained partial knowledge remain UNDECIDED. Previous suggestions that early Second Age founders knowingly preserve First Throne laws, records, dynastic claims or direct political succession are not canon.

CREATOR CONFIRMATION (2026-11-21): The Khazari awoke gradually across a 167-year span at the START of the Second Age's second Avarran era, the Era of Wonder: Second Age Years 322–488 inclusive (167 years). They had slept beneath the mountains since the Great Cataclysm, and the First Throne was magically forgotten. The First Throne kept very few conventional written documents because it developed an advanced magical method of writing OR of storing information directly in people's minds, rendering routine written documentation obsolete except for special cases; surviving ordinary written documents would mainly be very old, predating the system, or special-purpose. Whether the actual mechanism is magical writing, mind-storage or a hybrid remains UNDECIDED. Do not canonize a particular storage medium or how it failed. Earlier early-Second-Age active Khazari rebuilding narratives must be revised to reflect the slumber.

CREATOR PROPOSAL (2026-11-21, tentative and revisable): First Throne magical information technology may have originated as TWO distinct disciplines—magical writing and magical memory/storage in minds—subsequently fused into an integrated knowledge-preservation system. One or both source magics, or only the fusion technique, may have been lost during the Great Cataclysm and magical forgetting. Exact survival/loss pattern is NOT decided. Assistant working labels 'Runic Inscription', 'Mindbinding' and 'Living Archive', and any detailed capabilities, are illustrative proposals only, not canon. Avoid choosing a loss outcome without creator confirmation.

CREATOR DECISION (2026-11-21): Canon: First Throne developed TWO distinct magical information disciplines, magical writing and magical memory, then FUSED them into the advanced archival system that rendered conventional documents largely obsolete. The FUSION TECHNIQUE WAS LOST following the First Throne's fall/Cataclysm. Preserve BOTH previously discussed historical possibilities: some knowledge may be lost with dead living custodians, while ancient external magical archives may remain intact yet inaccessible because the fusion cannot be reproduced. The independent disciplines may have survived in whole, fragmentary or altered form; their exact survival and mechanics are not yet established. Working names 'Runic Inscription', 'Mindbinding' and 'Living Archive' remain noncanonical placeholders.

CREATOR RESOLUTION (2026-11-21): The First Throne's fused magical-writing/magical-memory technique was lost SPECIFICALLY THROUGH THE MAGICAL FORGETTING, not because the Great Cataclysm physically destroyed the technique or its archival substrates. The Cataclysm and slumber remain connected historical events; exact mechanics of forgetting and which independent disciplines survived remain undecided. Previously speculative alternative that the Cataclysm itself severed the fusion is superseded.

CREATOR CANON CORRECTION (2026-11-21): First Throne archival systems must remain ACCESSIBLE in principle to Khazari without personal magical ability: non-magical dwarves existed even in the First Age, so the civilization's information infrastructure was not restricted to mage users. Distinguish access/use from ability to invent, fuse, repair, reproduce, or fully understand the two original magical disciplines. The magical forgetting erased knowledge of the writing-memory fusion, but did NOT categorically render all surviving archives unreadable or inaccessible. Some archives may remain hidden, sealed, damaged, restricted, or difficult to understand; exact non-magical interface and operating rules undecided. Supersedes earlier speculation that all intact archives were inaccessible solely because fusion knowledge was lost.

records.title: Southern Wastes Dark Mages
records.summary: At the start of the Era of Fire, communities exiled mages who had accessed dark magic.
records.body: At the start of the Era of Fire, communities exiled mages who had accessed dark magic. The mages gathered in southeastern Avarra, destroyed fertile farming land by magic, created a volcano and lived in isolation without external diplomacy or trade. The mages survived far into the Third Age. Their identities and ultimate fate remain open.

records.title: End of Second Age — Global Earthquakes
records.summary: In Second Age Year 1,437, planet-wide earthquakes struck Eryndor.
records.body: In Second Age Year 1,437, planet-wide earthquakes struck Eryndor. The already ancient Ironspine mountain ring amplified and transmitted aftershocks approximately tenfold globally. Extreme-western Avarran lowlands rose into new mountains; these are not the Ironspine. Many individuals perished, but no existing species was wiped out. An unnamed magic helped prevent extinction; its mechanism remains open.

records.title: The Created Southern Volcano
records.summary: Created by the dark mages at the start of the Era of Fire.
records.body: Created by the dark mages at the start of the Era of Fire. The end-of-Age earthquakes intensified it. Mages harnessed and restrained its potential eruption, limiting destruction but unknowingly increasing their own magical power. The intervention does not guarantee there was no eruption, damage or death.

Hidden or unusually inaccessible inland water body enclosed by the Ironspine ring, with shore settlements. Its precise magical concealment and possible lunar relation remain unresolved.

CREATOR'S NEW HISTORICAL DIRECTION (2026-11-21; under development): The First Throne was a vast subterranean Khazari empire centered in the Ironspine Mountains. The inland sea enclosed by the mountain ring is linked to a mysterious magical harness or power system that the First Throne learned to use. Its exploitation precipitated the Great Cataclysm and the empire's fall. The catastrophe, the Silence Below and the eastern mine are to have connected histories; precise mechanisms, sequence, dates, and nature of the mine connection are deliberately undecided. The previously established multiple-moon collision scenario is under revision: do not assert whether collisions caused the catastrophe or were caused by the harness until decided. This is a working historical direction, not license to invent missing details.

CREATOR CONFIRMATION (2026-11-21): The First Throne discovered an extraordinary naturally occurring magical power beneath the Ironspine Mountains, then engineered and constructed a vast artificial harness to exploit it. The inland sea is connected to this system, but its precise role (source, regulator, consequence, or other) remains undecided. Exploitation of the system ultimately triggered the Great Cataclysm and contributed to the empire's fall. The failure mechanism, lunar collision relationship, and eastern mine/Silence Below connection remain open; do not invent these details.

CREATOR CONFIRMATION (2026-11-21): The inland sea BOTH contains and naturally regulates the extraordinary magical power. Without any artificial harness it can accomplish wondrous things but remains unpredictable. The First Throne's Khazari sought to control and exploit that power; dwarven greed for mastery and power is a thematic cause of their overreach. The artificial harness's interference with natural regulation precipitated the Great Cataclysm and the empire's fall. Greed is an imperial motivation, not a universal moral property of all Khazari. Exact engineering, failure mechanism, moon collisions and mine/Silence Below linkage remain open.

CREATOR CONFIRMATION (2026-11-21): The eastern mine extends far deeper than its previously documented six public and nine private-survey levels; these are only upper portions of a far larger ancient First Throne installation. Every dwarven hold has a deep connection/passage leading toward a shared central convergence where the Great Harness machinery meets, associated with the magical inland sea. Knowledge is uneven: some holds/rulers know of the passages or their purpose, others know only fragments, and others are unaware. Do not equate the network automatically with ordinary trade Deepways or presume each route is presently traversable. Exact layout, convergence structure, depths, access, which holds know what, and security remain undecided.

Seven independent Ironspine mountain kingdoms linked by trade, diplomacy and Deepways; 132 million modeled domain residents combined, including 22.8 million in the Karak-Varn planning envelope.

CANON KHAZARI GEOGRAPHIC DISTRIBUTION (2026-11-22): The overwhelming majority of Khazari live in Avarra's Ironspine mountain system, the core homeland of the Seven Thrones. Only a few scattered pockets exist outside Avarra, primarily in some of the larger mountain ranges on other continents. Smaller Khazari settlements elsewhere within Avarra may exist, but no extensive overseas Khazari realm is implied. Exact percentages, population totals, and overseas settlement histories remain undecided pending demographic revision. The older 132-million Seven Thrones figure counts domain residents and must not automatically be equated to 132 million ethnic Khazari.

CANON KHAZARI DISTRIBUTION PERCENTAGES (2026-11-22): Of the WORLDWIDE Khazari population, 83% live in Avarra, including 74% living directly within the Ironspine mountain system and 9% elsewhere in surrounding Avarran regions; the remaining 17% live across other continents, principally in mountain ranges. These are percentages of the global Khazari population, NOT percentages of Avarra's population or of the 83% subgroup. Total worldwide Khazari headcount remains provisional pending demographic recalculation. Continuity review needed: the earlier description 'only a few scattered pockets outside Avarra' must be interpreted as geographically concentrated overseas settlements or revised, because 17% of the species is a significant minority. Do not invent overseas kingdoms or settlements without creator approval.

CANON OVERSEAS KHAZARI INDEPENDENCE (2026-11-22): Khazari communities located outside Avarra have NO ties whatsoever to the Seven Thrones. They are not politically subordinate, allied by formal obligation, tributary, or institutionally connected to any of the seven Avarran kingdoms. Their own histories, political structures, cultural practices and reasons for geographic separation remain to be developed independently; do not infer a shared overseas government or automatically assign migrations, diplomatic relationships, or Seven Thrones allegiance.

CANON LONGEVITY (2026-11-21): Typical natural lifespan 800–1,000 years. This is a typical range, not a hard maximum; exceptional ages are not yet specified. Physical maturity, legal adulthood, reproductive ages and cultural seniority remain to be defined separately; do not scale childhood proportionally to lifespan by assumption. Established Hammerfeld and other Khazari NPC ages remain unchanged pending any explicit revision. Long lives do not imply lowered birth rates or weakened family bonds. Multigenerational overlap and population implications warrant later demographic review; do not silently alter planning population figures.

CANON AGING PATTERN (2026-11-21): Prolonged physical vitality with gradual visible aging throughout adulthood, not perpetual youth followed by abrupt decline. Most of the natural lifespan can be physically active; signs of age and eventual decline emerge progressively and vary with individual health, genetics, lifestyle, injury and magic. Age cannot reliably be inferred precisely from appearance. This confirms the pattern only; previously proposed numerical maturity/adulthood/elder-stage boundaries and exceptional longevity limits are NOT yet confirmed.

CANON REPRODUCTIVE LONGEVITY (2026-11-21): Reproductive capacity typically continues through approximately the first two-thirds of a Khazari's natural life. With typical lifespan 800–1,000 years, this suggests an approximate end range of 530–670 years, with individual variation and gradual decline rather than an abrupt universal cutoff. The two-thirds figure refers to overall lifespan, not a mandate to reproduce continuously; onset depends on separately unresolved physical maturity. Do not automatically reduce established birth rates.

CANON ADULTHOOD (2026-11-22): Khazari attain full cultural and legal adulthood at age 30, with full independent adult rights and responsibilities. Earlier proposed physical maturity around ages 18–25 remains a working biological estimate, not yet separately confirmed. Working, apprenticeship, household residence and responsibilities before 30 are possible; legal adulthood does not compel leaving family homes. Existing character ages remain unchanged: Gloin 42, Bruni 57, Tovin 34 are adults; Elska 26 is below full legal adulthood, though may work as a clerk. Details of legal permissions for those under 30 vary by jurisdiction and remain to be developed.

CANON EXCEPTIONAL LONGEVITY (2026-11-22): Khazari with exceptionally long natural lives can reach approximately 1,300–1,550 years. Typical natural lifespan remains 800–1,000 years; ages 1,000–1,300 are unusually long-lived, with 1,300–1,550 extraordinarily rare. Such longevity need not imply magic or heroic destiny. Prolonged vitality and gradual aging still apply, including significant eventual decline. This range describes exceptional natural longevity, not a universal hard cap against magical life extension. No historical individual is retroactively assigned such an age.

CANON SHARED COMING-OF-AGE FRAMEWORK (2026-11-22): All seven Khazari Thrones retain ROUGHLY SIMILAR coming-of-age traditions, reflecting their shared ancient origin despite the magical forgetting of the First Throne. Their communities do not remember that ancestral source. Local rituals and interpretations can vary by Throne, but the broad custom remains recognizable across them. Full legal/cultural adulthood at age 30 remains established. Specific rites, names, symbols and principles (e.g., responsibility, contribution, ancestry) are proposed examples ONLY, not yet canon.

CANON THREEFOLD COMING OF AGE (2026-11-22): At age 30, Khazari full legal/cultural adulthood is marked by a shared, integrated coming-of-age tradition built on THREE inseparable ancestral principles: RESPONSIBILITY (readiness for independent duty and accountability), CONTRIBUTION (demonstrating or declaring how one will contribute to family/community/kingdom, without requiring a specific occupation or extraordinary accomplishment), and ANCESTRY (honouring preceding generations). These are facets of one rite, not three mandatory separate ceremonies. All Seven Thrones preserve recognizably related versions, with local symbols, ceremonies and celebrations differing. Their shared forgotten First Throne origin is not consciously remembered. Exact ritual format and any formal name remain to be designed.

CANON COMBINED COMING-OF-AGE PRINCIPLES (2026-11-22): The Seven Khazari Thrones share a broadly recognizable coming-of-age tradition combining ALL THREE principles: Responsibility (readiness to make decisions and answer for them), Contribution (a place or purpose within family/community/kingdom, not mandatory mastery or a particular profession), and Ancestry (honouring forebears despite magical forgetting of the First Throne). These are integrated aspects of one tradition, not three unrelated mandatory ceremonies. Full Khazari legal adulthood remains age 30. Exact ritual names, tests, symbols, and local differences remain undecided; individual Thrones may vary their expression while retaining the common principles.

records.title: Eldar
records.summary: Elves; ancient woodlands, art, scholarship and multiple independently evolving cultures.
records.body:
Elves; ancient woodlands, art, scholarship and multiple independently evolving cultures. Do not equate long lifespan with uniform birth rates or priorities.

Present-day planning population: 108,000,000. Numbers are planning values, not a sudden birth boom or immutable count. Every people has multiple cultures and communities; social roles and character cannot be deduced from species alone.

CANON LONGEVITY (2026-11-21): Typical natural lifespan 2,500–3,500 years. This is a typical range, not a hard maximum; exceptional ages are not yet specified. Physical maturity, legal adulthood, reproductive ages and cultural seniority remain to be defined separately; do not scale childhood proportionally to lifespan by assumption. Existing cultural and birth-rate principles remain in force. Multigenerational overlap and population implications warrant later demographic review; do not silently alter planning population figures.

CANON AGING PATTERN (2026-11-21): Prolonged physical vitality with gradual visible aging throughout adulthood, not perpetual youth followed by abrupt decline. Most of the natural lifespan can be physically active; signs of age and eventual decline emerge progressively and vary with individual health, genetics, lifestyle, injury and magic. Age cannot reliably be inferred precisely from appearance. This confirms the pattern only; previously proposed numerical maturity/adulthood/elder-stage boundaries and exceptional longevity limits are NOT yet confirmed.

CANON REPRODUCTIVE LONGEVITY (2026-11-21): Reproductive capacity typically continues through approximately the first two-thirds of an Eldar's natural life. With typical lifespan 2,500–3,500 years, this suggests an approximate end range of 1,670–2,330 years, with individual variation and gradual decline rather than an abrupt universal cutoff. The two-thirds figure refers to overall lifespan, not a mandate to reproduce continuously; onset depends on separately unresolved physical maturity. Do not automatically reduce established birth rates.

CANON EXCEPTIONAL LONGEVITY (2026-11-22): Typical natural lifespan remains 2,500–3,500 years. Unusually long-lived Eldar may reach approximately 3,500–4,500 years; extraordinarily rare naturally long-lived Eldar may reach 4,500–5,500 years. Prolonged vitality, gradual visible aging, eventual natural decline, and reproductive capability for roughly the first two-thirds of individual natural lifespan remain unchanged. Exceptional longevity does not by itself imply magic, high status, or royal ancestry. These are natural-life ranges, not an absolute prohibition on extraordinary magical longevity. The 1,437-year Second Age could be witnessed in full by a single Eldar, while the 8,873-year Third Age cannot be spanned by one naturally lived Eldar life. Historical eyewitness possibilities depend on actual birth dates; do not retroactively invent witnesses. Birth rates and planning population remain unchanged pending separate demographic review.

CREATOR DEVELOPMENT NOTE (2026-11-22): Eldar cultures' distinct coming-of-age traditions will be developed later; do not prematurely impose a single shared ceremony or pick an Eldar adulthood age without confirmation. Distinct Eldar cultural practices remain open.

CANON ELDAR MATURITY (2026-11-22): Physical maturity develops approximately between ages 25 and 40; full legal and cultural adulthood begins at age 75 (creator selected Option C). Eldar may study, apprentice, travel and assume increasing responsibilities between physical and legal maturity. Distinct Eldar cultures will have different coming-of-age customs; their exact ceremonies remain deliberately deferred. This does not change typical lifespan 2,500–3,500 years, exceptional lifespan 4,500–5,500 years, gradual aging, or reproductive longevity.

CANON MATURITY AND ADULTHOOD (2026-11-22): Creator chose Option C: Eldar reach physical maturity approximately ages 25–40 and attain full legal/cultural adulthood at age 75. Eldar aged 40–74 can be physically mature, educated, employed and responsible without having all legal rights of a 75-year-old; jurisdiction-specific rules remain undecided. Cultural coming-of-age ceremonies may differ across Eldar societies; their individual ceremonies are deferred, but 75 is the common adulthood benchmark. These rules coexist with typical 2,500–3,500-year lifespan, exceptional 4,500–5,500-year lifespan, gradual aging, and fertility lasting roughly two-thirds of life. No existing character ages or birth rates are changed.

CANON AVARRAN ELDAR HOMELAND (2026-11-22): Letharion Forest is the major homeland of Avarran Eldar. Three separate Eldar clans are situated respectively in the Veridian Expanse, the Silent Mangroves, and the Miredeep (the user referred to this last region as 'the more deep'; map labels it THE MIREDEEP, Bound Wetlands). Clan names, size, governance, relationship to Letharion, and wider Eldar distribution remain undecided. Do not infer that these three clans are the only Eldar communities in Avarra.

CANON AVARRAN ELDAR POLITICS (2026-11-22): Letharion Forest contains MORE THAN ONE independent Eldar kingdom, including one major kingdom (name and precise structure not yet established). The three separate Eldar clans based in the Veridian Expanse, Silent Mangroves and Miredeep are politically independent. Each has a loose alliance or relationship of alliance with the major kingdom in Letharion Forest, but the three clans have NO formal alliances with one another. Do not conflate loose alliances with subordination or a united Eldar state. Names, boundaries, and any other ties remain undecided.

CANON LETHARION KINGDOM COUNT (2026-11-22): Exactly THREE independent Eldar kingdoms exist within Letharion Forest: TWO large kingdoms and ONE smaller kingdom. One of the two large kingdoms is the previously established major kingdom maintaining separate loose alliances with the independent Eldar clans of the Veridian Expanse, Silent Mangroves, and Miredeep. The clans have no formal alliances with one another. Kingdom names, borders, relative populations, relations among kingdoms, and the smaller kingdom's influence remain undecided.

CANON LETHARION HALF-BROTHER RIVALRY (2026-11-22): The rulers of Letharion's TWO large independent Eldar kingdoms are exceptionally long-lived Eldar kings who are HALF-BROTHERS. One king is born outside marriage (bastard-born); which king, the shared parent, their names, ages, succession rules and legal ramifications are not established. Their kingdoms are longstanding rivals under a currently existing petty truce, characterized by continued competitiveness rather than genuine reconciliation. Do not assume the truce ends war forever, that the smaller third kingdom takes sides, or that bastard birth automatically invalidates the king's rule. The kings' exact longevity and how long they have personally ruled remain undecided.

records.title: Avarra — Second Age Annals
records.summary: Awakening: River-Stone Breadhouses, Court of Four Weirs, Lantern Refuge.
records.body:
**Avarra • Second Age Years 1–1,437.** This is newly developed **revisable canon** building on the old Ironspine, diverse independent peoples, the Two-Hand Rule, the Eldar Living Calendar, and the later Year 1,322 Southern Wastes catastrophe. Avarran names Awakening, Wonder and Fire are **local historical convention**. New ancient polities do not automatically become the present Seven Thrones, Aldermere, Valtoria, merchant republics or Eldar High Sovereignty.

## The first generations — the Receding Certainties (Years 1–113)

### The Night of Unlit Steps

On several old mountain roads, signal runes that had been reliable over many generations became misleading. In the high valleys, **the Night of Unlit Steps** refers to a succession of fatal wayfinding accidents when messengers, haulers and rescuers followed glimmering markers toward unsafe ground. It was not one simultaneous magical failure across Eryndor. Khazari stone-carters responded by driving physical stakes into slopes, carving ordinary route marks and maintaining lamp stores that no enchantment was required to light. Some masters gave the work to apprentices, whom they did not always credit; an apprentice named **Heska Rellstone** became locally renowned for insisting that the people who cleared dangerous roadways deserved the same share of memorial honors as famous runesmiths. In subsequent years some halls adopted a **workroll of the living**, listing cooks, healers, porters and stone carriers beside engineers. Others refused.

This sharpened a wider cultural argument at the roots of the **Two-Hand Rule**: should a work be admired for its brilliance if ordinary workers were forced to die when it failed? The debate was carried by multiple independent guilds and families, not an edict from a known future Throne. The Ironspine already existed, ancient beyond First Age.

### The River-Stone Breadhouses

In a westward river belt, a coalition of grain merchants, Goblin drovers, Human farmers, Halfling growers and some Troll ferry families built **the River-Stone Breadhouses**: ordinary granaries and ovens maintained with verifiable inventories. They were a pragmatic response to spoiled magically preserved stores. Members contributed food in times of abundance and could seek rations in famine, but there were bitter conflicts over strangers' eligibility. One overseer, **Talen Vey**, secretly sold emergency flour to creditors; discovery of the theft provoked public hearings and the appointment of rotating stock auditors who did not share a family estate. The reforms succeeded in some communities and failed in others. An elderly Ogre widow remembered as **Rhuma of the Low Ford** earned renown for ferrying families through floodwater without asking them to present citizenship marks first. Her name survives in folk accounts of different reliability, not an unbroken contemporary archive.

### The woodland grief and the Living Calendar

The western woodlands recovered unevenly from altered lunar influences. Some Eldar keepers watched orchards cease flowering on expected nights; others found old groves thriving under the planet's distinct World's Breath. Under **Curator Aelthira of the Fern Courts**, several forest schools shared seed archives and daylight-based observational records rather than treating rare botanical knowledge as the property of one lineage. A powerful competing circle prohibited seed sharing with outsiders, citing thefts of sacred cuttings and real danger to their forests. Young Eldar, Satyr gardeners, Ent witnesses and Pixie settlements argued over how protection became exclusion. One small archive was deliberately burned during an argument over water access; the new **Vow of the Second Copy** required a participating school to entrust a duplicate to a neighboring community, ideally one outside its own household. This vow was voluntary and sometimes broken. It was a Second Age innovation, not a surviving First Age record.

## Recovery under imperfect laws (Years 114–321)

### The Court of the Four Weirs

A riverine government called the **Court of the Four Weirs** governed several irrigation basins, toll crossings and towns, with local assemblies only partly represented at its royal court. Its early court was credited with opening floodgates during an ill-timed storm; its later officials began selling rights to the same water. **Judge Neral of Northbank**, a human law officer whose household was supported by Halfling farmers and Goblin accountants, attempted to make **public flood marks** admissible evidence against royal water-mages. The court's debate became known as the **Argument of Dry Stone**: when magic and visible water levels disagree, which may a judge trust? The resulting law required measurement and witnesses in some districts. It did not abolish corruption, and neighboring independent states ignored it.

### The Lantern Refuge and its betrayal

A mixed riverside sanctuary founded by Kobold ventilators, Gnome craft teachers, some Brownie households and displaced market families sheltered people unable to pay urban rent. Its rules prohibited forced labor in exchange for immediate rescue. Years later, a council faction began attaching predatory service contracts to admission. **the Lantern Petition**, carried through market towns by a coalition of children, workers and elders, forced a public accounting and restored shorter terms. Some freed workers never recovered lost years; their survival is part of the history, not proof the settlement was always benevolent.

### Goblin roads and Ogre jurisdictions

Goblin communities were not one traveling nation. Some lived permanently in the cities of the Court of Four Weirs, some kept mountain-edge gardens and workshops, and others moved seasonally between distant markets. The **Salt-String Caravans** carried news of unsafe bridges, suspicious coin and counterfeit warding stones along routes that no kingdom completely controlled. In some provinces, Ogre quarry towns held recognized local courts and trade scales; elsewhere, strong-armed robber bands and human rulers alike exploited isolated roads. The memories of these incidents do not explain later anti-Goblin or anti-Ogre prejudice through Orc wars: there were **no Orcs in the Second Age**.

## Wonder's opening — power available, but not equally (Years 322–550)

### The Hall of Common Measure

At a meeting of otherwise rival Khazari craft houses and Gnomish instrument makers, a demonstration showed how a magnificent new lunar enchantment could hide cracks in an ordinary support beam. They founded **the Hall of Common Measure**, an experimental meeting place and training network rather than a single mountain kingdom. It offered affordable mechanical inspections alongside magical certification. Foremen liked the reduced risk; enchanted-tool monopolists despised its pricing. Some apprentices forged certificates, causing injuries and scandal. Afterward, **the Three-Witness Trial** required three independent accounts of a critical test: from a magical practitioner, a physical examiner and a user of the device. That practice spread unevenly.

### A court that starved its own villages

A prosperous western lowland principality, **the Briar-Crown March**, financed monumental enchanted roadways by requiring grain levies from rural districts. The roads were beautiful, shortened trade and enriched urban patrons. During several poor seasons, communities paying the levy went hungry. A coalition of rural tax assessors, Pigfolk bakers, Cowfolk growers, Human fieldworkers and Foxfolk couriers organized the **Thousand-Bowl March**: an unarmed procession carrying empty bowls to the principality's gate. Guards assaulted protesters and several died. The prince's successor eventually reduced levies and established village appeal hearings, less through charity than fear of further revolt. The roadways' surviving maintenance cost became a byword for splendid projects built on neglected people.

### The forest of divided gifts

Several Eldar grove schools developed impressive new moon-fragment arts of growth, light and healing. One made medicine available to nearby settlements at low cost; another restricted it to households that accepted permanent custodianship by the court. Ent councils opposed reckless clearing but were divided on whether intervention against unjust forest lords was their duty. Some Aelwyn Fae offered protection on conditions their neighbors found impossible to understand. No Faerie group is automatically Eldar, Pixie or Brownie. The **Open Glade Letters** were an agreement among a few woodland teachers to teach basic botanical medicine without demanding a lifetime oath. They did not end secrecy everywhere.

## Wonder's middle centuries — rivalry, reform and memory (Years 551–920)

### The Toll-Bell War (Years 604–607)

At three competing waterways west of the old Ironspine, the Briar-Crown March and two self-governing market leagues fought a **regional war over tolls and river access**. The war included warehouse burnings, short sieges, river skirmishes and deliberate damage to public canals. It did **not** involve Orcs, the later isolated dark mages or the undated east–west war tradition. A widow's coalition collected the names of missing boatmen across political lines. Their **Bell of Returned Names** was rung whenever a prisoner or displaced person returned home. The negotiated **Greywater Terms** limited wartime seizure of grainboats; subsequent rulers sometimes violated them. Hope was not the absence of war, but ordinary people forcing enemies to acknowledge their shared dependents.

### The buried-house debate

Among independent Khazari communities the wealthy **Stone-Claim Houses** argued that the heirs to a discovered abandoned hall could inherit its machinery and secrets. Opponents insisted that spaces full of dangerous devices should be surveyed and made safe before property claims. The argument produced **the Seven Lantern Inspections** across seven sites—not seven modern Thrones. Some halls were sealed, some reopened, and one excavation was abandoned after fatalities. Their builders and ancient dates remain **unknown**. This is not evidence the abandoned sites belonged to the First Throne or that Gloin descends from anybody associated with them.

### The years of wandering teachers

Gnome lecturers, Merfolk current-watchers from shore markets, Halfling agronomists, Goblin legal clerks and independent Human healers circulated testable instructions that wealthy guilds tried to license. **the Roadbook of Errors** became a compilation of failed devices, spoiled crops, mislabeled spells and narrow escapes, deliberately recording mistakes alongside successful techniques. Some rulers banned it as an insult to their prestige. Copies survived because traveling families and workshop elders made duplicates. The book was written within the Second Age, not retrieved from the undocumented First.

## Wonder's later years — joy and its price (Years 921–1,321)

### The Nine Hearth Hospitals

A group of independent community hospitals, commonly called **the Nine Hearth Hospitals**, formed across several Avarran market areas; “nine” refers to an early association, not a sacred count of civilizations. Their patrons included rival merchants, women from once-indebted households, healing practitioners and practical supply keepers. Some hospitals offered new lunar-derived healings, but their plain water, food, clean linens and trained care mattered equally. One major patron demanded that debtors be refused aid; a worker coalition threatened to close the hospitals rather than enforce the rule. Their refusal won a limited charter reform and cost several workers their positions.

### Late forests, contested towns

Long-lived Eldar witnessed both the Awakening's emergencies and the flourishing of Wonder; some grew confident in protective magic and disliked younger critics who questioned their monopoly over gardens. In the eastern and western lowlands, mixed settlements often succeeded because their markets accepted several peoples' legal practices without requiring identical beliefs. Other towns built walls, excluded outsiders and enforced harsh debt laws. The ability to hide an enchanted settlement did not make its inhabitants universally virtuous or free of internal abuse.

### The southeastern farmland before the Wastes

The area that would later become the **Southern Wastes was still fertile, lived-in southeastern Avarran farming country through Second Age Year 1,321**. Its residents were not knowingly cultivating a natural desert around a pre-existing volcano; the volcano **did not yet exist**. Regional farm councils, landlords, irrigation workers, family holdings, market hamlets and ordinary religious practices were diverse. Nothing here predetermines the identities or fate of every household in the later catastrophe. Some local records that survive in later copies preserve debates over irrigation and marriage inheritance; no authentic First Age record is hidden among them.

## Avarra during the third era (Years 1,322–1,437)

The **dark mages** were exiled at the beginning of the era, gathered in southeastern Avarra and **created** both the Southern Wastes and their volcano with dark magic. They did not negotiate alliances, trade or diplomacy with pre-existing outside peoples. The **Ashward Flight**, **Crown of Three Fords and Queen Merea**, **Hearth-Gate Agreements** and **Grove-Court of Seralith** are established in the separate Era of Fire — Kingdoms, Peoples & Cultural Chronicle (Second Age, 1322–1437). Their political history is **not** silently backdated into Wonder. At the end of Year 1,437 the world earthquakes amplified by old Ironspine changed far-western Avarra's landscape, magnified volcanic danger, and ended the Second Age. No species went extinct; losses were terrible; the sustaining magical force is still unresolved.

## Inheritance and limits

These new chronicles establish particular ancient courts, guilds, movements, wars and family customs but **do not imply any modern state was founded in the Second Age**. Neither the First Throne's exact dates nor the Silence Below nor Gloin Hammerfeld's ancestry has been settled. The old Ironspine and the newly raised mountains at the western tip are distinct. Modern urban populations and current census totals are not given ancient values. Other continents' era terminology is not imposed by Avarra's historical narrative.

records.title: Tharvorn — Second Age Annals
records.summary: Awakening: First Salt-Winter, Cedar-Peg Routes, Lady Haldra of Veskhar Reach, Three-Bell Settlement.
records.body:
**Tharvorn, Second Age Years 1–1,437 in Avarran retrospective dating.** Tharvorn's own era names and internal calendar boundaries are **not yet established**. The date bands below allow cross-continental comparison; they do not impose the Avarran names Awakening, Wonder or Fire on Tharvorn's people. This is new **creator-authorized, revisable** regional history.

## A coast where old light could no longer be trusted (Years 1–115)

Tharvorn's fjord dwellings, upland halls, forest villages and storm coasts did not experience the post-Cataclysm world equally. A ward protecting a boathouse might work on one night and fail on the next. In the **First Salt-Winter**, a succession of local storms and delayed fish runs brought hunger to several independently governed coast communities. The name is retrospective and refers to **regional weather and supply breakdowns**, not an extra planetwide moon-shattering event. Some lords requisitioned boats and forbade independent fishers from landing catch; a few villages divided stores by household need, sometimes against their governors' orders.

Among the first efforts at ordinary, verifiable rescue were **the Cedar-Peg Routes**, a system of carved wooden storm markers, stepped cairns and manually maintained shelters. Wolvenkin trail families, Bearfolk caravan houses, Troll river builders, human boatmen, some Giants and cliff-dwelling Harpies all participated in different places. Not all were allies, and certain local chiefs regarded rescue corridors as unauthorized passage over their land. One northern town hanged a guide for sheltering travelers without charging an official winter toll. His sister, **Mava Stone-Lantern**, later helped organize the **Gate-Side Table**, where decisions about shelter duty were recorded publicly.

### The Four Smoke Lodges

Several unrelated forest and highland settlements negotiated a practical **Four Smoke Agreement**: each lodge would maintain a physical smoke beacon, a winter store, a messenger route and a spare shelter key, rather than trust a single protection spell. One participating Giant household offered enormous roof timbers but demanded rights over nearby quarry access; some smallfolk councils considered the price exploitative and found other builders. The resulting compromise made timber a paid trade rather than a hereditary tribute. This was no universal Giant–Human treaty and no origin charter for the modern Northern Holds.

## The reign of thaw and debt (Years 116–321)

The coastal lordship of **Veskhar Reach**, a narrow collection of ports and neighboring farms rather than all Tharvorn, grew rich by granting privileged whaling, fishing and saltwork licenses. Its ambitious **Lady Haldra of the Quays** funded stone breakwaters and nonmagical navigation lights; she also allowed lenders to seize the working boats of families with unpaid winter debts. Her own court records portrayed her as a savior, while harbor workers remembered the **Winter of Locked Oars**, when boats sat idle as hunger spread.

A guild of boat repairers, led in part by **Jorven Ash-Wake**, an elderly human master, and **Urrek Flintfoot**, a Troll timber fitter, refused to repair seized ships without written release of their crews. Guards assaulted them; some were imprisoned. The strike produced **the Three-Bell Settlement**, a limited harbor rule permitting independent review of seizure after storms. The new rule did not erase old suffering or end debt bondage everywhere. Children of imprisoned workers later became respected pilots and union-minded shipwrights, not simply inherited victims.

On the forest margins, Troll families retained distinct rites around river crossings, and Bearfolk lodges debated whether food stores should be shared with neighboring villages. Some Foxfolk traders were prized for fair winter contracts; others exploited isolation. Forest keepers from Eldar, Ent and smaller woodland communities fought over whether a dangerous path should be cleared or closed for the season. There was no uniform moral alignment among them.

## Flourishing under new moons (Years 322–618)

As moon-fragment powers became better understood, **the Straits of Twin Lanterns** became a maritime region notable for thriving trade routes and scholarly lodges; the name describes two prominent physical navigational lights, not two newly invented moons. Ports built combined observation towers and ordinary beacon networks. Some schools used lunar arts for ice warnings and wave sensing while keeping weatherbooks, depth ropes and trained shorewatchers. Merfolk observers exchanged current readings with harbor crews, but underwater polities retained the right to decline surface contracts.

The small **Sea-Glass College** sponsored experimentation in weather prediction, healing, metals and winter navigation. Its high fees excluded fisher households until **Master Sivi Redd**, a Gnome instrument maker, established an independent public teaching workshop that demonstrated low-cost alternatives. Several wealthy scholars mocked the small instruments; her students successfully predicted a dangerous shoal season using mundane observations in combination with lunar measurements. When the college attempted to acquire the workshop, dockworkers and students kept it independent. This was a victory for access, not proof that every coastal school became generous.

### Giant sky courts and reluctant guests

Highland Giant speakers gathered at **the Rock-and-Star Moot** to debate safe passes and hillside quarrying. Some used renewed magical observation to protect lower villages; others refused cooperation, claiming that newcomers were draining ancient upland resources. A dispute involving a collapsed shelter was resolved by a work levy paid partly by large-house quarry interests rather than forcing poorer valley households to provide unpaid labor. The Moot was one regional political culture, not the government of all Giants.

## The hard peace of the coast (Years 619–960)

A short regional conflict known as **the War of the Beacon Keys** broke out among competing small maritime lordships over ownership of lights, salvage rights and the ability to deny passage. Port militias set fires in warehouses and confiscated winter stores. A partially enchanted beacon failed after being tampered with, and ships wrecked because captains had trusted its signal. The war never involved Orcs, the southern Avarran mage exiles or the global east–west wars of undated later history.

The end came through the **Harbor Witness Compact**, negotiated by rival boatbuilders, Merfolk navigators, some Harpy coastal scouts and grieving fishing families. Its best-known clause prohibited any signatory harbor from deliberately displaying a false safety light, even during war. A few captains obeyed it at enormous personal cost; later rulers broke it. The compact nonetheless became a model for subsequent port laws and a reminder that an agreement can matter even when it fails to end every abuse.

Meanwhile, winter medicine developed in inland valleys. A Bearfolk physician, **Era Vennpine**, organized the **Blue-Snow Houses**, public huts stocked with dry linen, salted broth and simple medical supplies. Their use of permitted lunar healing was celebrated, but they did not require magical practitioners for every rescue. Some landowners objected to feeding people traveling without permission; several huts were burned in reprisals, then rebuilt from donated timber. No whole species is cast as invariably kind or unkind.

## New prosperity, old divisions (Years 961–1,321)

Tharvorn's last centuries in Avarra's “Wonder” date band saw competing northern successes: trade cities enriched by steel, timber and harbor tolls; small coastal settlements sustained by mutual shelter; rich courts commissioning enchanted winter gardens; and miners injured in profitable mountain excavations. A succession crisis in Veskhar Reach, now only one of several rival port powers, exposed how fragile hereditary claims were. A council of merchants tried to replace a disputed child claimant with an oligarchic regime; work crews demanded representation and limited their ability to rule by credit alone. The **Harbor Assembly of Eight Benches** gave each of several occupational constituencies a place to speak, though it still excluded many people and did not transform every port.

The **Archive of Lost Crews** collected accounts of vanished fishers, guides and prisoners across decades, preserving names of the poor alongside nobles. Unlike impossible First Age archives, its source documents arose in the Second Age itself. Some names were transcribed incorrectly; volunteers kept corrections visible rather than invent false certainty.

### The people beneath the chroniclers' headings

Human towns were not all sailor kingdoms; Wolvenkin neighborhoods included scholars, farmers, soldiers and couriers; Bearfolk families varied from solitary homesteaders to busy political households. Troll merchants could be fair or violent. Giant circles disagreed over land and sacrifice. Harpy flights were independent cliff and port communities, not a universal warning corps. Gnome, Goblin and Halfling households built permanent lives in selected areas rather than passing through for other peoples' benefit. Merfolk communities sometimes restricted surface access for good reasons. Drakari visitors, if any in a particular dispute, are **not** automatically given a role, a named patron or a throne.

## The late Second Age (Years 1,322–1,437)

The **Frost-Hearth Confederation** and **Red-Lantern Custom** in the existing Era of Fire — Kingdoms, Peoples & Cultural Chronicle (Second Age, 1322–1437) represent a **later** northern rescue tradition, not a rename of the earlier Four Smoke Lodges or Harbor Witness Compact. They can share practical values without being the same continuous institution. The ending global earthquakes harmed places far from their origin, but no precise Tharvorn casualty census or destroyed capital is fixed here. No species went extinct. Tharvorn's own names for these periods are still to be decided.

records.title: Sahrad — Second Age Annals
records.summary: Awakening: Dry Steps, Brass-Well Kingdom, King Issaret, Queen Naluma, Waterkeeper’s Chains and Open Well Decree.
records.body:
**Sahrad • Second Age Years 1–1,437 in Avarran retrospective dating.** Sahrad's local eras, reign counts and cultural historical names are still **undecided**. This new chronicle deepens river, savanna, caravan, coast and desert societies. No modern Sultanate or royal line is automatically dated to the Second Age.

## The first broken channels (Years 1–135)

After the Great Cataclysm ended the undocumented First Age, certain lunar works governing water and navigation became unreliable. This was catastrophic in some settlements dependent on them, but no two valleys were required to fail the same way. On a section of the **Sahradi River**, villages remembered **the Dry Steps**, a sequence of seasons when canal levels no longer matched predictions. Farmers dug emergency bypasses while wealthy households purchased rights to functioning wells. At **the Stone Jar Landing**, an independent town council forced sellers to mark the water they sold by ordinary measured volumes rather than by magical promises alone.

An Elephantfolk waterwright, **Ammara of the Deep Gauge**, and a Human surveyor, **Meret Saref**, collected flood marks and hand-drawn channel charts. Their work, preserved in **the Book of Unfaithful Wells**, described failures openly without pretending to restore First Age texts. Some city officials destroyed copies, embarrassed by proof they had sold water they could not guarantee. Village children and itinerant potters recopied the markings on ordinary clay; this is one reason the work survives in incomplete later copies.

In the broad savannas, Centaur households disagreed about seasonal pasture claims, while Lionfolk and Minotaur town councils argued over who could cross communal reserves during drought. A few disputes became violent; others ended in paid access, negotiated seasonal movement or joint watch parties. No continent-spanning animal-people monarchy resulted.

## The Brass-Well Kingdom (Years 136–321)

A regional **Brass-Well Kingdom**, centered on a chain of river settlements and caravan junctions, rose through management of water allotments, salt trade and grain prices. Its ruler **King Issaret the Patient** ordered the making of public well records and built mundane reservoirs. His successor **Queen Naluma of the Sealed Courtyard** invested in moon magic that worked splendidly in a few gardens, yet allowed creditors to hold indebted farmers to life-consuming labor contracts.

The scandal remembered as **the Waterkeeper's Chains** began when a group of rural households showed that their entire harvest had been pledged repeatedly against the same unpaid canal repairs. Workers sabotaged a tax register; soldiers retaliated by taking relatives hostage. A coalition of Elephantfolk accountants, Human laborers, Lionfolk advocates and Goblin caravan clerks petitioned royal magistrates. The resulting **Open Well Decree** made some emergency drinking water exempt from debt seizure. It did not abolish class hierarchy or end all bondage. Former hostages were not simply restored to their old lives; several later founded **the Quiet Reed House**, an independent refuge with no requirement of royal allegiance.

In southern marshlands and coastal deltas, Merfolk and river port communities measured separate risks. Surface rulers coveted privileged underwater routes and sought restrictive contracts; several Merfolk councils refused them. Others traded voluntarily, often negotiating from strong independent positions.

## Prosperity and its shadows (Years 322–590)

New lunar-derived arts enriched navigation, irrigation, agriculture and medicine. Sahrad's **House of Five Bowls**, a scholarly hospital and teaching network established across several cities, became known for combining practical diet, sanitation, nonmagical care and careful observation with newly reliable lunar healing. Its training halls admitted pupils from different peoples but charged fees that excluded many rural families. A Lionfolk healer, **Yashel Varn**, established a free courtyard for apprentices who agreed to teach outside the capital afterward. The charity struggled to survive and relied on donations from merchants who expected favorable public honors.

The Brass-Well Kingdom's later rulers were weakened by succession disputes and water shortages. Some towns became independent; others accepted governors from new powers. The kingdom was **not** transformed automatically into the later Blue-Jar Crown (which belongs to the final 116 years) or the present Southern Sultanates. Differences in architecture and inheritance law persisted after political change.

### Savanna courts and wandering law

A loose **Circle of Grazing Stones** linked independent Centaur communities and nearby pastoral and farming settlements around routes, sacred gathering places and water rights. In some circles, a mobile delegate could challenge the decision of a permanent landholder; elsewhere hereditary chiefs dismissed such claims. **Speaker Denna of the Wide Crossing**, a Centaur mediator, prevented one grazing dispute from becoming a much larger war by guaranteeing alternative seasonal access. Her agreements were negotiated, local and vulnerable to later violations.

## The Saffron Gate Disputes (Years 591–790)

A competing inland caravan polity, **the Saffron Gate Dominion**, grew wealthy by licensing passage between wells and taxing luxury spices and ordinary water alike. Its governor **Sethen of the Closed Hand** turned debt failure into hereditary servitude on several roads. This policy produced forced migrations, banditry and resistance. The **War of the Scattered Seals** was a limited conflict among caravan city governments and resistant corridor towns. Soldiers burned storage yards; displaced families lost their tools and names were erased from some official records. This was not the Second Age's end, not an Orc campaign and not a war with the isolated Southern Wastes mages, who had not yet gathered.

The most notable resistance came from **the Unsealed Caravan**, an alliance of merchants, freed workers, caravan guides and water carriers. An Elephantfolk legal instructor, **Veshara Nul**, drew up **the Free-Water Claim**, insisting that emergency drinking water could not be pledged as property. The Dominion called the claim rebellion; a few towns adopted it after difficult bargaining. It freed some families and brought reprisals against others. The caravan endured as a name for practical mutual aid, not a single bloodline or tribe.

## The long arguments of Wonder (Years 791–1,115)

Not every city was drawn into the Dominion's conflicts. Independent savanna and coastal realms supported art, mathematics, temple scholarship, song, medicine and international trade; others financed magnificent observatories while neglecting sanitation. One coastal **Hall of Contradictory Stars** taught astronomers to record mutually inconsistent moon sightings rather than force them into a neat divine system. Priests from different cults, skeptical navigators and Fae interpreters argued heatedly there. Its collections were **Second Age** observations and not proof of authentic First Age records.

In urban Lionfolk neighborhoods, some schools favored public service, others aristocratic honor and still others quiet domestic obligation. Minotaur advocates disagreed about whether a city's justice should be enforced by strong guardians or independent judges. Elephantfolk households included scholars, craftworkers and political reformers alongside waterwrights; no shared instinct for perfect memory was assumed. Pigfolk cooks, Cowfolk farmers and Foxfolk market families could achieve status, suffer discrimination or become officials in individual towns. Merfolk coastal enclaves retained their own trade policy and civic institutions.

## Late Wonder: the Tenth Granary Trial (Years 1,116–1,321)

An unusually costly urban grain project became famous as **the Tenth Granary**. It promised stores protected by powerful new lunar methods; its sponsors neglected ordinary pest control, structural checks and equitable distribution. A badly managed season caused spoilage and hunger among tenant districts while the elite's stores remained intact. Rather than conceal the failure, **Inspector Adira the Ledger-Keeper**, a Human magistrate, released the failed inventory and requested testimony from workers whose warnings had been ignored. Witnesses faced threats and several fled, but the evidence brought **the Open Storage Hearings**, which required manual inspections and public granary accounting in participating towns. The reform was imperfect and local, yet a generation later it saved lives when another stored crop failed.

Religious movements about generosity and water purity flourished alongside severe temple tolls and splinter sects. No single deity, new universal lunar source or continent-wide conversion is specified. This history preserves both real repression and everyday joys of gardens, marriages, markets and festivals that continued despite it.

## The last 116 years and the Age's end

The **Blue-Jar Crown**, its water-rights hearings and **Dispute of the Seventh Gate** belong to the existing Era of Fire — Kingdoms, Peoples & Cultural Chronicle (Second Age, 1322–1437) as a **later regional state**; this text does not identify it with the Brass-Well Kingdom or the Saffron Gate Dominion. At the end of Year 1,437, the earthquakes devastated communities around the world and ended the Second Age. Exact Sahradi losses and the protective magic's workings remain unresolved; **no species was wiped out**. Nor did Sahrad itself become the Southern Wastes: those magically formed in **southeastern Avarra**.

records.title: Orundel — Second Age Annals
records.summary: Awakening: Lost-Stair Flood, Chain of Safe Boats, Reed-Gold Assembly.
records.body:
**Orundel • complete Second Age in Avarran retrospective Years 1–1,437.** The names and boundaries of **Orundel's own historical eras remain undecided**. This chronicle places distinct river, tropical woodland, highland, steppe and maritime societies in shared time without pretending they were one kingdom. It predates, and does not duplicate, the **Reed-Crown League and War of Three Locks** established for the final 116 years.

## A river that could no longer be read (Years 1–110)

As the Great Cataclysm reshaped lunar power, communities around the river mosaics of Orundel struggled to anticipate floods. Some ancient magical signs were not merely weak but actively misleading; other local workings remained functional, and the World's Breath continued independently. **The Lost-Stair Flood**, remembered in a cluster of towns but not a global disaster, caught lowland residents where a protective water ward failed. A group of Tigerfolk medicine apprentices, Human boatbuilders and Goblin ferry families opened a disused warehouse as a clinic. The clinic's founder, **Saluma Reed-Hands**, was a Human boatwright who insisted that free beds be counted by available space rather than by a magistrate's caste register. A local governor later tried to charge the clinic for harbor frontage. Neighbors protected it by linking boats across its landing, creating the custom of **the Chain of Safe Boats**.

In the upper forests, Mushroom folk investigated changes in rot, soil and water by direct study, not a collective hive mind; Gnomes worked alongside them on drainage. Their first **Living Soil Notebooks** recorded what they could actually observe. Some human settlers blamed fungus communities for ordinary blight and destroyed several gardens, even when the gardens had supplied food during shortages. An independent **Shade Court**, formed by a handful of resident households of different peoples, heard testimony and ordered reparations from some attackers; other communities never saw justice.

## Roads between unlike worlds (Years 111–321)

### The Reed-Gold Assembly

A network of river towns developed **the Reed-Gold Assembly**, a rotating meeting of independent ports that agreed on physical flood marks, emergency boat access, river weights and seasonal taxes. It did not rule the whole continent; inland plateau cities, rainforest federations and Centaur steppe societies had their own rulers. Voting was unequal, favoring wealthy ports. **the Silt-Marked Petition** was prepared by a group of poorer boat crews, Harpy scouts, and Foxfolk legal clerks who demanded that disaster crews receive a legal voice. The Assembly adopted a limited right to testify without granting equal political votes.

A Tigerfolk cartographer, **Neris of Seven Bends**, developed river charts combining current soundings, physical landmark sketches and recently observed lunar conditions. Her rival claimed she had stolen techniques from a less prestigious Merfolk navigator. Her surviving annotations credit several Merfolk and Goblin collaborators, making her celebrated work also evidence that famous single authors often depended on unrecognized people.

### The highland refuge quarrels

In upland regions some Giant, Kobold and Human communities argued over access to stone shelters during changing weather. A mountain lord turned several refuges into toll houses; a Kobold family called **the Red-Handle Builders** enlarged ventilation shafts and enabled trapped families to escape when a ward misfired. An independent Minotaur mediator, **Karrum Vale**, negotiated a new contract that paid maintainers and required emergency shelter for travelers. That agreement lasted for two generations before a later ruler ignored it. Its failure did not erase the lives it had saved.

## Early Wonder: a thousand directions (Years 322–575)

Different Orundel towns grew rich as newly mastered moon-fragment arts improved botanical knowledge, metalwork, civic architecture and navigation. The **House of Patient Rivers** was a riverside teaching college open to many occupations, though fee waivers depended on guild sponsorship. A group of students organized **the Night Lessons**, teaching calculation, law and medicine to workers after market hours. Several teachers were dismissed; some joined a newly chartered public school and helped create practical health instruction independent of patrons.

In tropical forest regions, **the Rain-Bark Confederacy**, a loose alliance of villages and forest councils, limited clearing of certain watersheds after a series of damaging floods. Not all villages agreed: some wanted more farmland and suspected the restrictions protected powerful timber traders. Ent witnesses advised some council gatherings, but they did not rule the communities, and Aelwyn rites of reciprocity remained separate. A forest healer, **Vasha Half-Sky**, criticized both wealthy clearers and elites who forbade the poor to gather medicines. Her **Gatherer's Measure** granted seasonal access to specified plants without opening sacred groves to wholesale destruction. It was a negotiated compromise, not a universal law.

### The great demand for copper light

A guild of Gnome, Goblin, Human and Tigerfolk artisans developed intricate safe-light systems, pairing new lunar enchantments with ordinary oil and repair access. Their lamps enriched port life, theater, schooling and night medicine; temple and noble interests sought monopoly licenses. **the Copper-Light Walkout** followed when miners and glassworkers objected to pay withheld for equipment alleged to be magically perfected. Workers' threatened strike led to a partial accident-compensation schedule. It left large inequalities intact, but made public the names of people previously listed merely as workshop property.

## Mid-Wonder: the price of straight roads (Years 576–910)

### The Green-Step Principalities

Small, competing principalities on the forest-steppe transition financed causeways and enriched trade through dense river markets. Their rulers varied: elected councils, hereditary houses, military commanders who kept temporary rule for too long. These were **not** modern Orundel kingdoms renamed, and they did not form one universal empire. In the eastern steppe, Centaur associations negotiated rights of passage and irrigation with settled farming villages; some cases ended in open councils and others in punitive fighting.

A prince in one Green-Step state began seizing land from mixed communities to build a grand enchanted highway, claiming new lunar engineering would make agriculture unnecessary along the route. Farmers, including Pigfolk, Cowfolk, Goblin and Human households, resisted through petitions. A few organized armed defense and were beaten; surviving witnesses called this episode **the Four-Market Suppression**. One governor later restored some fields when a neighboring city refused to buy grain seized under the decree. The reversal was incomplete, but it marked the beginning of **the Bounded Works Statute**, requiring public assessment of a major construction project's effects on local water and farms. Skilled engineers could support the statute without being enemies of magic.

### The Amber Ledger Trials

In a southern river city, trade officials falsified measures for ore and medicine and blamed bad magic when shortages appeared. **Magistrate Eren Kha**, an independent Human judge, took testimony from a Merfolk pilot, a Foxfolk auditor, several wounded dockhands and a Mushroom folk apothecary. Their evidence exposed an organized fraud. Witnesses were threatened, and the first trial was annulled after political interference. A later public inquiry made independent scales and river sampling mandatory at some docks. Corruption survived elsewhere, and the affected families carried losses that no verdict fully repaid.

## Late Wonder: universities and broken charters (Years 911–1,321)

The **Six Rivers Symposium** brought scholars and practical workers from different parts of Orundel together to compare rival medical and lunar-magical claims. It did not appoint a universal master of magic. Tigerfolk and Gnome researchers, Centaur astronomers, Lionfolk legal thinkers, Merfolk current observers and other people held incompatible theories. A prominent patron demanded that results be hidden from competing cities; a group of graduate teachers circulated a **Public Ledger of Failed Cures** anonymously, helping healers recognize unsafe practices. Court officials prosecuted some contributors; others preserved their findings in open clinics.

In the highland margins, Kobold and Giant builders found work alongside other peoples and also faced exploitative contracts. Harpy cliff towns developed independent warning signals, theater and local political contests, not simply messenger jobs for city kings. Different Mushroom folk councils contested whether medicinal fungi should be freely shared or locally controlled. A village grew prosperous on new lunar farming techniques, while a neighboring family unable to afford training lost its land to creditors. Such contradictions were typical: the broadly prosperous millennium had space for terrible injustice.

### The weather-watchers' promise

After a major storm damaged several unrelated ports, river scouts, Merfolk current keepers and Harpy watchers established **the Promise of Open Warning**: a local obligation to share imminent danger information even with rival towns. The policy saved many travelers and was sometimes broken for strategic advantage. Its imperfect legacy later influenced river warning practice without being declared the foundation of the **Reed-Crown League** of Years 1,322–1,437.

## The final Avarran date band (Years 1,322–1,437)

The **Reed-Crown League**, its internal political differences, and **War of Three Locks** are recorded in the existing Era of Fire — Kingdoms, Peoples & Cultural Chronicle (Second Age, 1322–1437). They are independent of the Green-Step Principalities and the Four-Market Suppression unless later creator decisions establish a relationship. The world-shaking earthquakes of Second Age Year 1,437 ended the Age; **no species went extinct**. A full regional death toll, exact Orundel states destroyed, and the name locals gave this era remain open. **There were no Orcs in Second Age Orundel**.
